stories.headline: Nepal flash flood kills 100, leaves hundreds missing; earthquake-avalanche link under probe
stories.title: Nepal flash flood kills 100, leaves hundreds missing; earthquake-avalanche link under probe
stories.summary: At least 100 people have been killed and hundreds remain missing after a devastating flash flood swept through Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts along the Tibet border on Wednesday, with officials warning that the death toll could rise as rescue teams reach cut-off areas. The Nepal Tourism Board (NTB) said 384 travellers were preliminarily reported missing, including 291 foreign nationals and 93 Nepalis. The figures are still being verified, with authorities cross-checking records with travel agencies, guides, local administrations and security agencies. According to The Himalayan Times, at least 105 Indian nationals and 37 non-resident Indians (NRIs) are among those reported missing. The number of Indian nationals could increase as verification continues. The NTB said 59 of the Indian nationals were travelling through Samrat Tours & Travels and 46 through Leaf Holiday, while the 37 NRIs were listed separately under Himalayan Glacier. The preliminary list also includes foreign travellers from the UK, Malaysia, the US and South Africa. The flood struck the Bhote Koshi River at around 8.30 am, sweeping through parts of Rasuwa before affecting the Trishuli River and settlements in Nuwakot. Nepal Police said 114 people have been rescued from the Bhotekoshi River area in Rasuwa, where flash floods struck on Wednesday, according to local media. The Nepal Army rescued more than 80 people by helicopter, while private helicopter companies rescued another 29, Nepal TV and Radio Nepal reported. Earthquake may have triggered avalanche A possible chain of events behind the disaster has emerged, with Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal telling Parliament that preliminary information indicated an earthquake at around 8.37 am triggered an avalanche, which in turn caused the flash floods. Khanal stressed that the information was still being verified. He said China’s Tibet region had also suffered “huge damage” and that Nepal was coordinating with Chinese authorities. The minister said 26 police personnel, nine armed police personnel and 44 military personnel were missing. Customs and immigration officials were also among those unaccounted for. There has been extensive damage to roads, bridges, communication networks and hydropower infrastructure, with Rasuwa and Nuwakot the worst affected districts, Khanal said. Earlier, Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology had said the flooding was not caused by heavy rainfall. Less than seven millimetres of rain had been recorded in Rasuwa over the previous 24 hours, prompting authorities to examine other possible causes, including a glacial event. Buildings collapse, bridge swept away The scale of the destruction has emerged through verified videos reviewed by the BBC. Footage from the Trishuli Bazaar area of Nuwakot, about 25 km north-west of Kathmandu, showed the river suddenly swelling with huge volumes of fast-moving, sediment-filled water. A bridge was swept away by the force of the floodwaters, followed moments later by the collapse of several multi-storey buildings. Other footage showed the aftermath, with trees and buildings near the riverbank washed away, partially collapsed or covered in thick layers of mud and debris. The flood also reportedly swept away around 60 houses near Trishuli Bazaar and damaged two motorable bridges. District Police Office chief Bipin Regmi said three unidentified bodies were recovered from the Trishuli River bank in Nuwakot — two at Simchaur and one at Kolputar. At least 17 people have been rescued so far. The Nepal Army said 12 people were evacuated by helicopter — six from Syafrubesi, two from Mailung and four from Dhunche. Four Army and eight private helicopters have been mobilised for search and rescue operations. Security personnel, officials among missing Fourteen employees of the Rasuwa Customs Office in Timure also remain out of contact, including 11 permanent and three contract staff. Twenty-five other employees, including Chief Customs Administrator Rajendra Dhungana, have been accounted for, according to Nepal’s Finance Ministry. The disaster has disrupted roads and bridges, making access to some affected areas difficult. Five people stranded by the flood were rescued and taken to Chakradev Hospital in Bidur, while access to Trishuli Hospital was disrupted after roads and bridges were washed away. The flood also damaged the Trishuli and Devighat hydropower projects and swept away three blocks and a substation of a 25-MW solar power plant. Travellers remain unaccounted for The large number of missing travellers has added a major international dimension to the disaster. The BBC quoted a Chinese businessman based in Kathmandu, Yee Liang, as saying his logistics company had seven container trucks in the affected area, all staffed by Nepali employees. “We have lost contact with all of them. There is no signal, so we cannot reach anyone,” he said. Yee said he was not aware of any warning before the flood. “There were occasional mudslides and landslides, especially in the rainy season, but this one seems much more serious,” he told the BBC. On the Tibetan side, Guan Daoxuan, based in Sichuan province, told the BBC that he had lost contact with his wife, who works for a state-run construction company involved in building roads and bridges in Tibet. Chinese state media have reported “major casualties” from a mudslide at a trade hub on the Tibetan side of the border. Chinese President Xi Jinping has called for an “all-out” search for missing people and stronger monitoring and early-warning systems to prevent further disasters. Rescue and relief operations intensified The Nepal government has mobilised the Nepal Police, Armed Police Force, Army and district administrations for search, rescue and relief operations. Prime Minister Balendra Shah has directed government agencies to ensure close coordination, while President Ram Chandra Paudel called on government bodies, political parties, social organisations and citizens to intensify rescue efforts. The World Health Organization is preparing medicines and equipment for around 1,000 people, along with 15 emergency tents. Nepal’s Health Ministry has reserved 100 emergency beds at Bir Hospital and the Trauma Centre in Kathmandu and deployed medical teams to support the operation. With many areas still inaccessible and hundreds of people unaccounted for, officials are continuing to verify casualty and missing-person figures. The death toll is therefore expected to remain provisional until search teams can reach the worst-hit areas. PM Modi speaks to Nepal counterpart, assures all possible assistance Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday spoke to his Nepalese counterpart Balendra Shah following the deadly flash floods in parts of Nepal and assured him of India’s “all possible humanitarian assistance”. PM Modi conveyed his condolences over the loss of lives and said India stood in solidarity with the people of Nepal during the crisis. “Spoke to Prime Minister Balendra Shah and conveyed condolences on the loss of lives due to the floods in Nepal. The people of India stand in solidarity with their sisters and brothers in Nepal at this difficult time,” Modi said in a post on X. He added that India was coordinating “closely on rescue and relief efforts” with Nepal.

article_sentences: Nearly 160 people were killed and over 750, including 133 Indians, remain missing after a massive flash flood triggered by an earthquake in Tibet swept through central Nepal, devastating towns, washing away bridges, crippling hydropower projects, and leaving widespread destruction across multiple districts.

Kathmandu: Nearly 160 people were killed and over 750, including 133 Indian nationals, remain missing after a massive flash flood originating in Tibet swept through central Nepal on Wednesday, devastating several towns and villages, washing away critical bridges, and crippling a dozen hydropower projects.

Nepal Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told the parliament that an earthquake hit the Tibet region at 8:37 am (local time) and the flash floods were reported three minutes later, suggesting the tremors may have caused a glacial outburst which triggered the floods.
The flood surged through the Bhote Koshi River affecting Rasuwa and Dhading districts bordering Tibet, officials said.

The massive flood entered the Trishuli River through the Bhote Koshi in Timure, a border-town in Rasuwa district, due to the rockslide and swelling of the Lhende River situated along the Nepal-Tibet border, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.
It then spread along the river course to other districts like Nuwakot, Chitawan, Gorkha, Tanahu and Nawalparasi East, covering areas ranging from around 70 km to nearly 200 km from capital Kathmandu.
The Nepal Police in a social media post said 157 people died in the flash flood that hit the Himalayan nation.
The Nepal government said around 500 were missing, while China’s state-run CGTN news channel said three people were dead and 265 were missing on the Chinese side of the border.

Videos from the affected areas showed a powerful surge of muddy water, rocks and debris sweeping through the border region, with people seen fleeing as the torrent moved towards buildings and vehicles.
In one clip, a four-storey structure could be seen being swept away by the raging waters, while another showed a car floating in fast-moving floodwaters in Rasuwa.
Another video clip showed a long bridge broken into two by the sheer force of water.
Other video clips showed bridges being pounded by powerful currents before collapsing and being swept away.

stories.title: Rasuwa border flood underscores need for stronger regional cooperation on climate risks, HKH lawmakers say
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A deadly flood in Nepal’s Rasuwa border district has sharpened calls from Hindu Kush Himalaya lawmakers for stronger regional cooperation on climate risks.

At the 2nd HKH Parliamentarians’ Meet in Bhutan, speakers urged collective action, climate-smart laws and investments, and cross-border preparedness to protect vulnerable mountain communities and downstream populations across the eight-country region.

The devastating flood in Nepal’s Rasuwa district along the Nepal-China border underscores the urgent need for stronger regional cooperation to address climate risks that transcend national boundaries, parliamentarians from across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region said on August 26, 2026.

The lawmakers were speaking at the 2nd Hindu Kush Himalaya Parliamentarians’ Meet in Thimphu, Bhutan, according to a statement by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD).

Participants said the disaster highlighted the importance of collective action, stronger preparedness, and sustained regional cooperation to reduce climate-related risks and build resilience across the HKH region.

The two-day meeting, taking place from August 26 to 27, brings together legislators from across the region to exchange experiences, discuss emerging climate risks, and explore how policies, legislation, and public investments can better support adaptation and resilience.
Opening the meeting, Deputy Speaker Sangay Khandu of the National Assembly of Bhutan stressed the role of parliamentarians in turning climate commitments into action.
“Resilience cannot live in scientific reasoning anymore or in the speeches of ministers and government officials or members of parliament.
It cannot live only in the commitments we make at the global stage,” he said.
“Resilience should be carefully woven into the fabric of our laws, our budgets, our institutions and our actions on the ground.
It is parliamentarians who have the power to ensure it.”
Participants highlighted that climate risks are increasingly affecting communities across borders and require coordinated responses that go beyond national efforts.

article_sentences: Shortly after the flood struck Gyirong on Wednesday, the Isha Foundation founder said 77 pilgrims from one of his Kailash pilgrimage groups were at an immigration centre there.
The group, which was returning from the Kailash pilgrimage, had stopped at the centre when floodwaters surged through the building.

Spiritual leader Sadhguru Jaggi Vasudev on Thursday appealed to Chinese authorities to allow him and a small team of volunteers to travel to Gyirong, Tibet, to help search for 80 pilgrims who went missing after a devastating flash flood swept through the town bordering Nepal.
In an appeal to the authorities, Sadhguru said he was writing “in absolute pain” over "losing 80 people from our group in the floods in Gyirong.
We have no further information after the floods."
Sadhguru said he and the families of the missing pilgrims were requesting permission to travel to Gyirong, where they wanted to assist in the search.
“We deeply respect and understand the nature of the rescue efforts and will in no way hamper them.
Our only intent is to stand with them and aid in looking for some signs that would help the families,” he said.

stories.headline: Japan Struggles To Attract Solar Bids, Lessons For India
stories.title: Japan Struggles To Attract Solar Bids, Lessons For India
stories.summary: A Mature Market Running Out of Easy Sites Japan added 5.8 GW of solar in 2025, a respectable pace for a land-constrained, densely built country, but the most recent auction data suggests the Feed in Premium tariffs (FIP) mechanism itself is straining. Unlike the older feed-in tariff system it replaced, FIP tariffs are explicitly designed to shrink over successive rounds as a maturing market is expected to need less support. The problem is that Japan's remaining greenfield sites are disproportionately the difficult ones, be it mountainous terrain, land-use conflicts, or locations requiring costly grid upgrades. A shrinking premium on top of that is making marginal projects harder to underwrite. Developers appear to be sitting out rounds rather than bidding at tariffs that no longer work out. Recent Auction Seven companies split just a third of the capacity Japan put up for bids in its 29th solar auction, extending a run of undersubscribed rounds that offers some pointers perhaps for India's own auction economics. Japan's power auctioneer awarded just 38.2 MW out of 115 MW put up for bidding, continuing a run of undersubscribed rounds that is starting to look less like an anomaly and more like a pattern in one of the world's most mature solar markets. And one might add, well paying ones. The Organization for Cross-regional Coordination of Transmission Operators (OCCTO) said that of the seven companies that split eight winning bids for projects of at least 250 kW, AC12 took the largest share at 29.9 MW; Sandia, Japan Petroleum Exploration and Solar Field 13 rounded out the rest. The weighted-average winning tariff came in at ¥8.89 (~Rs 5.32)/kWh, just under OCCTO's ceiling price of ¥9.6/kWh. A clear sign that competitive tension in the auction was thin rather than fierce. The shortfall is not new. Of 13 business plans submitted for eligibility screening, only eight bids totalling 38.2 MW were ultimately submitted with some developers who cleared the eligibility bar simply chose not to bid the full amount they qualified for. Japan's 26th auction saw a similar pattern: 163 MW offered, only 75.4 MW awarded to 16 companies, a 46 percent fill rate. The 27th auction produced a lower weighted-average tariff of ¥4.61/kWh on a smaller pool of interest, and the 28th awarded 89.2 MW across 29 bids. Four consecutive rounds, four undersubscribed outcomes. The Indian Contrast And Future Pointers India's own auction experience has run in almost the opposite direction for most of the past decade: SECI and state-level tenders have typically been oversubscribed, with tariffs falling because competition for capacity remained intense even as the ceiling prices themselves were reduced round over round. India added a record 27 GW of solar in the first half of 2026 alone, and the country's tariff discovery process has generally been treated as evidence that aggressive price competition and high participation can coexist. But the conditions that produced Japan's fall-off, namely, a maturing pipeline, shrinking premiums, and constrained sites are not unique to Japan, and India is not immune to the same mechanics showing up later. MNRE Secretary flagged this month that nearly 42 GW of solar capacity is struggling to find offtake buyers, with grid curtailment eating into project economics in the same states that pioneered the low-tariff auction model. If ceiling prices in future Indian rounds are set without enough regard for the deteriorating economics of curtailment-exposed, storage-less capacity, the same undersubscription pattern Japan is now living through is not just a hypothetical risk but a real possibility.

India defeated Germany 1-0 in the FIH Pro League last year, securing its first victory over Germany in regulation time in 10 years.
Deepika scored the only goal of the game in the 12th minute, converting India’s first penalty corner and giving her side an early lead.
Germany had opportunities to respond, but India’s defence stood firm.
Goalkeeper Bichu Devi was particularly impressive, producing a series of important saves from both Penalty Corners and open play.
In midfield, India’s players repeatedly disrupted Germany’s rhythm, winning possession, battling for space and cutting off attacking avenues.
India also had chances to extend its advantage.
The best came in the 24th minute when Sharmila Devi found herself unmarked in a one-on-one situation, only to shoot straight at the German goalkeeper.
Despite missing opportunities to put the game beyond Germany’s reach, India managed to protect its narrow lead until the final whistle.
The victory was especially significant for India because it came against a German side that had traditionally been a difficult opponent.
It also lifted India off the bottom of the Pro League table and gave the team three valuable points.
That result will be fresh in the minds of both teams when they meet again at the World Cup.

stories.headline: India's Plan To Solarise Govt Buildings Mixed With Myriad Challenges
stories.title: India's Plan To Solarise Govt Buildings Mixed With Myriad Challenges
stories.summary: “Gujarat issues tender to solarise government buildings with rooftop solar.” Swap in Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, or any of a dozen others, and the headline still reads true — India has been running an almost continuous rotation of state-level rooftop solar tenders for government buildings through 2026. Rajasthan’s RRECL floated 33 MW in January. REIL, a central PSU, tendered 17.5 MW spanning multiple states the same month. NHPC issued 16.64 MW for central ministry buildings in February and another tranche for Sikkim, Manipur and Nagaland in May. Uttarakhand’s UREDA followed with 6.5 MW in June, Maharashtra’s MEDA has been quietly tendering primary health centres district by district, and UP’s UPNEDA issued 11 MW just this week. Nearly all of them use the same template: RESCO mode, tariff-based competitive bidding, a 25-year power purchase agreement, and roughly nine months from signing to commissioning. What almost none of them come with is a follow-up. Tender notices are routine, well-publicised and easy to track. Completion data is not. The handful of disclosures that do exist — mostly forced out through legislative questions rather than volunteered in press releases — suggest the gap between announcement and execution is wide, and wider in some states than others. THE NATIONAL NUMBER, THREE WEEKS OLD The clearest recent data point is a Lok Sabha answer from August 5, 2026. Responding to a question on rooftop solar mandates for government offices, the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy disclosed that it had received Action Plans for solarising 41,972 Central Government buildings, of which 24,376 — about 58 percent — had actually been solarised, adding up to roughly 854 MW. States and Union Territories, taken together, reported 81,754 government buildings solarised with a cumulative capacity of about 1,447 MW. Notably, the ministry could not or did not supply the denominator for the state figure — there is no total eligible-building count against which to measure that 81,754, which makes it impossible to compute a comparable completion rate for states the way the Centre’s own 58 percent can be computed. The same answer contained a smaller but telling admission: no Central Financial Assistance is available for rooftop solar on government buildings, because MNRE considers such installations “financially viable... even without CFA.” That assumption does a lot of work in explaining what follows. WHERE THE GRANULAR NUMBERS EXIST Karnataka is the one state that has put a hard number on the record recently, and it is stark. According to the state Energy Department, nearly 59,000 government buildings could together generate 698.2 MW of rooftop solar. As of this month, only 2,624 buildings — under 5 percent — have actually been fitted, totalling 33.68 MW, itself under 5 percent of the technical potential identified. A senior official acknowledged the shortfall directly, pointing to funding constraints and the absence of subsidy support for institutional buildings as the core blockers — essentially confirming, from the state side, the gap the Centre’s own no-CFA policy leaves open. Madhya Pradesh offers a useful before-and-after. In June 2025, Chief Minister Mohan Yadav announced that all government buildings in the state would carry rooftop solar by the end of 2025. That deadline has now passed with no completion announcement to match the original promise; the only recent capacity figure attached to Madhya Pradesh, 566 MW, refers to nearly 1.5 lakh residential PM Surya Ghar installations, not government buildings, and cannot be used as a proxy for the CM’s pledge. Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu occupy a middle position: MNRE has repeatedly named them as states “performing well” on government-building solarisation, most recently in a March 2025 ministry statement that also noted Chandigarh and Daman & Diu had reached full saturation of their government-building targets. But “performing well” is a qualitative label, not a disclosed percentage, and none of the four states appears to have published a Karnataka-style ratio of buildings solarised against buildings eligible. Gujarat’s own public figure — 2,451 government buildings solarised, from a 2024 state report — has no accompanying denominator either, so it is impossible to say from the public record whether Gujarat’s position as a stated leader reflects a genuinely higher completion rate or simply a larger base of early installations from a state that has run solar policy since 2009. WHY THE GAP EXISTS Three structural threads run through the disclosures that do exist. First, the financing assumption: MNRE’s position that government buildings don’t need Central Financial Assistance because RESCO tariffs are self-liquidating collides with the reality that RESCO payments still have to clear government budget-approval cycles, which move slower than a developer’s working-capital timeline. Second, net-metering and billing integration with DISCOMs remains a persistent friction point at the point of commissioning — an old but illustrative Himachal Pradesh case saw completed rooftop systems left non-functional for want of a working billing interface with the state board. Third, the CAG’s broader audit findings on renewable energy projects — including a specific finding that Coal India had covered only 4.08 percent of its 3,000 MW solar mandate by December 2024, with rooftop work orders issued for just 34.56 MW — point to a pattern of delay at every stage from planning through execution across public-sector renewable projects generally, not just rooftop-on-buildings specifically. None of this means the tenders are cosmetic. RESCO structures, competitive tariffs and 25-year PPAs are the correct mechanism, and the steady tender flow shows states are still actively working the pipeline rather than letting it lapse. What it does mean is that the tender is the visible, low-friction 10 percent of the process, and the commissioning, metering and reporting that follow are where the programme is actually tested — and where almost no state volunteers data unless a legislator forces the question. WHAT TO WATCH INSTEAD OF THE NEXT TENDER For anyone tracking this beyond the headline, the signal is not the next state to issue a tender — that is close to guaranteed to happen again within weeks. The signal is the next legislative answer or RTI response that discloses a completion number against a stated target, the way Karnataka’s assembly and the August 5 Lok Sabha reply did. Those are still rare enough that each one is worth a story in its own right, and collectively they are the only real audit trail this programme currently has.

stories.headline: India, China agree on eight measures to improve border management
stories.title: India, China agree on eight measures to improve border management
stories.summary: India and China have agreed on a series of measures to improve border management, maintain peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and advance negotiations for a settlement of the boundary question, following talks between National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing. The 25th round of talks between the Special Representatives (SRs) of India and China on the boundary question was held on August 25. Doval, India’s Special Representative, and Wang Yi, China’s Special Representative, held a “candid and in-depth” exchange of views and reached an eight-point consensus. Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining peace and tranquillity in the border areas and creating conditions for the stable development of bilateral relations. They also agreed to advance negotiations on a framework for resolving the boundary dispute in line with the 2005 Agreement on Political Parameters and Guiding Principles and subsequent understandings reached during the SR talks. As part of the effort, the Expert Group on Boundary Delimitation and the Working Group on Border Management under the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination (WMCC) will begin discussions on an “early and substantial harvest” on boundary delimitation and border management. Their first task will be to finalise their respective terms of reference. India and China also agreed that situations arising on the ground would be addressed promptly through existing diplomatic and military channels, including the WMCC and local commander-level meetings, to prevent misunderstandings and miscalculations along the LAC. The two sides agreed to establish two additional meeting points for General-Level Mechanism/Senior Highest Military Commander meetings. They also agreed on two additional channels for military hotlines in the Eastern and Middle Sectors to improve communication between the two militaries. Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, border trade The two sides noted progress in trans-border cooperation. India welcomed China’s decision to increase the number of batches of Indian pilgrims undertaking the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra in the Tibet Autonomous Region. Both sides also welcomed the reopening of three designated border trading points and agreed to strengthen cooperation in border trade, pilgrimage and other areas. They said the objective was to create an atmosphere of dialogue, peace, consultation and cooperation in the border areas. India and China further agreed to hold the next meeting of the Expert-Level Mechanism on Trans-border Rivers in September and continue discussions on issues including hydrological data sharing and renewal of relevant memorandums of understanding. The two sides also decided that the 26th round of Special Representatives’ talks will be held in India in 2027.

stories.headline: The story behind the English translation of Gulabnama
stories.title: The story behind the English translation of Gulabnama
stories.summary: Gulabnama is the biography of Maharaja Gulab Singh, the founder of the Dogra dynasty of Jammu and Kashmir. Originally written in Persian by Diwan Kirpa Ram, the work chronicles the establishment of the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir in 1846 and traces the life and political career of Maharaja Gulab Singh. It offers valuable insights into his statecraft, administrative policies, and the strategies he employed to consolidate and safeguard the frontiers of his kingdom during a turbulent period. Initially, Maharaja Gulab Singh was reluctant to have his life documented, fearing that sensitive family matters and personal details might be made public. For this reason, he was unwilling to entrust the task to the court historian, Ganesh Das Badhera. Instead, the responsibility was later assigned to Diwan Kirpa Ram, the son of Dewan Jawala Sahai, who served as Gulab Singh’s Prime Minister. The book faced significant hurdles in reaching the public. It took over a century for it to be accessible to common readers. Diwan Kirpa Ram completed the draft by roughly 1865-1866, but it was not printed until 1875 in Srinagar. It was finally published in 1875 at the Tofa Printing Press in Srinagar, Kashmir. However, it became rare quickly, and various attempts to translate it into English over next century were unsuccessful due to fundings, translation quality and institutional hurdles. Recognizing its historical importance, Raja Amar Singh, the father of Maharaja Hari Singh, wrote to Maharaja Pratap Singh in 1901, recommending that an annual budget of Rs. 500–1,000 be set aside for translating and publishing Gulabnama. Unfortunately, the proposal could not be implemented because no suitable translator could be found. A similar effort had earlier been undertaken for Kalhana’s Rajatarangini, which had been translated into English by M. A. Stein. The government sanctioned about Rs. 3,000 for that project, with nearly Rs. 1,500 spent on paper, printing, and distribution. This demonstrates the state’s willingness to invest in publishing important historical works. Professor Arnold of the University of Lahore was the first scholar approached to translate Gulabnama into English. However, after translating only the first sixty pages, he abandoned the project for personal reasons. The search for a competent translator continued. In 1902, Raja Amar Singh again approached Maharaja Pratap Singh, who constituted a committee to supervise the translation. Raja Amar Singh served as its President, while Diwan Diya Krishna, Bhagwan Narayan Das, and Dr. Suraj Bal were appointed as members. The committee engaged Babu Jagadish Chandra Banerjee to prepare an English translation for publication in Calcutta and paid an advance of Rs. 500. However, his translation was later rejected because it did not accurately reflect the original Persian text of Diwan Kirpa Ram. Another attempt was made during 1915–16 under Maharaja Pratap Singh, but it also remained unsuccessful. Later, efforts were made to translate the work into Urdu and Sanskrit, but these projects likewise remained incomplete. A major breakthrough came when Professor Sukhdev Singh Charak, Principal of Himachal Pradesh University, voluntarily undertook the English translation. He began the work in 1965 and completed it in 1976, devoting eleven years to the task. A benevolent man who appreciated the importance of the work offered Professor Charak a grant of Rs. 5,000. However, the total cost of publication was estimated at around Rs. 12,000. He was advised to seek financial assistance from the Jammu and Kashmir Academy of Art, Culture and Languages, but the Academy declined to provide funding. In 1975, Professor Charak was involved in a severe accident that left him critically injured. At the time, he felt that his survival was uncertain and that he might only have a few hours left to live. Facing what he believed to be the end of his life, he reached out to ensure that his life’s mission the translation of this book would be fulfilled. He even wrote a letter to a contact expressing that it was his final wish to have the book published. Fortunately, Professor Charak survived his injuries. Following his recovery, he returned to Jammu in 1976 to finalize the manuscript. The book was subsequently sent to the printing press later that year, finally appearing in 1977. The English translation of Gulabnama was formally released by Dr. Karan Singh, bringing to fruition a project that had witnessed more than seven decades of unsuccessful attempts. Author’s Note: This article was inspired by a YouTube video on The Dispatch by Zafar Choudhary. Hilal Ahmad Tantray, Research Scholar, Department of History and Culture, Jamia Millia Islamia, New Delhi.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court recently issued notice to the Delhi.
Police in a bail plea filed by co-accused Athar Khan in the 2020 North-East Delhi riots "larger conspiracy" case.
A bench comprising Justice Aravind Kumar and Justice Vipul M Pancholi issued notice in a special leave petition filed by Khan challenging the Delhi High Court's July 7 order denying him bail.
He was also denied bail by the Trial Court.
Athar Khan has sought bail on grounds of parity with Shadab Ahmad, who was granted bail by the Supreme Court in January 2026.

Khan was arrested in FIR No. 59/2020 under Sections 13/16/17/18 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967; Sections 302/307/353/186/212/395/ 427/435/436/452/454/109/114/147/148/124A/153A/120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.

It may be noted that a bench comprising Justice Kumar and Justice PB Varale has referred to a larger bench the question of understanding the 3-judge bench judgment in Union of India v KA Najeeb(2021), which held that long incarceration can be a ground to grant bail in cases under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act, regardless of the statutory rigours.
The reference was made while granting interim bail to co-accused Tasleem Ahmed and Khalid Saifi.

The reference came as a consequence to a judgment delivered by a two-judge bench(Justices BV Nagarathna and Ujjal Bhuyan) in Syed Ifthikar Andrabi, which criticised the judgments in Gulfisha Fatima and Gurwinder Singh (both authored by Justice Aravind Kumar), saying that they took a narrow view regarding bail in UAPA cases.
The bench in Andrabi took the view that Gulfisha Fatima and Gurwinder Singh departed from the KA Najeeb verdict.

stories.title: Rooftop Solar: The New Battle Between Vendors and Manufacturers
stories.summary: India's expanding residential rooftop solar market is going through its biggest change ever. Demand is strong thanks to the PM Suryaghar scheme, drawing in new players, while throwing up questions on the sustainability of the old model. The PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana has now crossed the 50-lakh-household mark, taking it halfway towards its target of one crore households (10 million) by March 2027. Registrations have already nudged 77 lakh. Delivering an installed capacity of 15.4 GW and subsidy disbursed of Rs 29,330 crore approx by Aug 15. Those impressive numbers will see a strong push for the next six months of the financial year. Who will capture the value created by that push? A strategic divide is beginning to emerge. The Two Camps On one side are traditional rooftop installers and service-led companies. They do not manufacture modules or inverters. Their proposition is built around acquiring customers, arranging financing, designing systems, installing them, managing approvals and providing after-sales support. This camp is also subdivided between the large mass of smaller sub 10-person firms, and the larger players who have strong regional and now, national reach as well. On the other hand are manufacturers that increasingly believe ownership of the hardware gives them a natural advantage. Module manufacturers are moving into rooftop EPC. Solar-pump companies are moving into modules, inverters and rooftop installation. Some are building their own retail networks; others are selling increasingly complete solutions through dealers and EPC partners. From none, until 2022, we have multiple firms offering solar kits today that include everything from modules to inverters to wires and even structures in cases. The battle between the new and the old is thus moving beyond the panel. It is about who owns the customer. The original thesis for this cover story was that the market is beginning to split between a service-first cohort and a manufacturing-led cohort. The underlying question is not which model is automatically superior, but where the durable margin will eventually sit: upstream, through control over the bill of materials, or downstream, through customer acquisition, financing, installation and retention. That distinction is becoming visible in the strategies of companies across the sector. Companies like Solar Square, Solarium, and Roofsol, which are focused primarily on the rooftop solar market, represent the clearest service-first proposition. Most of them have no manufacturing base (except Solarium, which just started manufacturing) and instead build around financing, installation, customer experience and after-sales service. Waaree Energies represents almost the mirror image, with its broader vertically integrated strategy and retail push attempting to take greater control of the rooftop value chain. Between the two, advertising is emerging as a clear indicator or the push to differentiate a commoditised market, especially for SolarSquare, while the manufacturing firms have leant on big ticket sponsorships and advertising in markets where their reach is strong. An industry veteran from a media buying agency estimates total solar spends of around Rs 800 crore rising between FY 25-26 and now. The rooftop sector would be 50% of that or Rs 400 crore on a segment turnover of over Rs 40,000 crore in FY 27. That’s barely 1% in a consumer facing segment with some heavy convincing to do. So far, it’s mostly the Prime Minister’s stamp and generous subsidy that has been the enabler. Even here, the key difference here is that service-focused firms are overwhelmingly B2C (Business-To-Consumer) and digital focused, unlike the manufacturing firms that have some B2B (Business-To-Busines) budgets as well. With exports to the US drying up, most would have stepped up domestic spending now. But the divide is not as clean as it first appears. Financing has emerged as a third axis. And then there are companies like Tata Power that have demonstrated that there may be another route altogether: control the brand, technology, supply chain, financing ecosystem and service standards while allowing channel partners to execute much of the last mile. Which explains Tata Power’s ambitious target to have 25% of the market by 2030 from 12-13% now, which would alone make it a Rs 30,000 crore segment in cumulative revenue for the integrated power firm. The service-first bet The traditional rooftop installer starts from a very different premise. It does not need to own a cell or module factory. Depending on a traditional dealer/distributor model, it sources modules, inverters and other components according to project requirements, counts on low working capital based on customer acquisition and advances. Installation methods and suppliers change as equipment prices and technologies evolve. In theory, this makes the business asset-light and flexible. The real investment is downstream. It is in acquiring the customer, explaining the economics of solar, arranging financing, primarily through NBFCs, designing the system, handling approvals, installing it correctly and remaining available when something goes wrong. This is particularly important because residential rooftop solar is a savings-linked product. The customer is not buying an abstract piece of renewable-energy infrastructure. Many of them are replacing part of their electricity expenditure with a solar asset and, increasingly, an EMI. That changes the importance of service. Swapnil Wakade , Business Head (Residential Solar Finance) of Ecofy, an NBFC, speaking to Saur Energy, put the issue bluntly: "service is the main thing in solar." His point was that the consumer ultimately cares whether the plant generates electricity and delivers the expected savings, regardless of the brand of module or inverter installed. That is also why financing companies are beginning to distinguish sharply between installer types. Swapnil says Ecofy has disbursed a good amount in residential solar over the past two years. Its experience has led it to favour larger and more established installers. "“There are a large number of smaller installers in the market, and ensuring consistent quality and service capabilities remains an important consideration for customers and financiers," Swapnil said, contrasting them with larger players that are building ecosystems intended to sustain the 20-25-year life of a solar system. That is not merely a question of reputation. It is a credit question. If a solar plant underperforms, the customer may no longer see the expected savings from the system. That can eventually become a dispute over the EMI. A number of NBFCs these days have also stopped onboarding very small installers unless they have completed more than 100 installations. The implication is significant: financing one of the forces driving sales could force consolidation in an otherwise fragmented rooftop market. Manufacturing's counter The manufacturing-led camp starts from almost the opposite position. It argues that the solar system is still fundamentally a hardware product, and whoever controls the hardware has greater control over cost, quality and supply. That matters in an industry where module prices can move rapidly and where changes in domestic-content requirements, ALMM rules or supply-chain conditions can alter the economics of an EPC project. The manufacturing-led model also offers an obvious attraction: margin capture at multiple stages. Instead of manufacturing a module and handing the customer relationship to someone else, a vertically integrated company can potentially manufacture the module, supply the BoS, install the system and provide O&M. Oswal Pumps has made this argument explicitly. On its recent investor call, Vivek Gupta , Managing Director (MD) of Oswal Pumps, explained that the company was participating in PM Surya Ghar as a manufacturer, producing modules, BoS components and mounting structures, while using its own sales channels for installation and supply. The objective, he said, was to earn margins across manufacturing and EPC rather than from a single layer of the value chain. The Karnal-based firm, which had created its brand in solar pumps and the PM-KUSUM scheme, has already started solar module production, plans to launch solar inverters in the next six months and has planned to use its solar dealer and servicing network to drive its rooftop solar services. It now eyes 2 lakh connections in FY 2026-27. Shakti Pumps is pursuing a related strategy, using its power-electronics background to build a rooftop business while simultaneously expanding into solar cell and module manufacturing. Its presentation describes a 2.2 GW DCR cell and module capacity and a growing dealer and partner network for the rooftop business. The Indore-based firm, which was primarily into the business of pumps and then solar pumps till now, thinks that once its in-house module and cell business starts, it would become one of the leaders in the integrated rooftop solar business, ultimately leading to higher margins for them. For these companies, rooftop is not just an adjacent market. It is an opportunity to extend an existing manufacturing capability downstream. And the results are overwhelming for the manufacturers too. For example, Shakti Pumps said that the revenues from their rooftop solar have also quadrupled albeit on a small base, hinting at the opportunities. “The rooftop business in this quarter showed a healthy growth. We clocked Rs 8 crores revenue as compared to Rs 2 crores in a like-to-like quarter last year. ” said Ramakrishna Sataluri, CEO of Shakti Energy Solutions, the rooftop solar arm of Shakti Pumps. GK Energy's more nuanced position GK Energy, another erstwhile solar pump firm with an asset light business model, offers an interesting variation because its argument is not simply that manufacturing wins. Chairman and Managing Director Gopal Kabra told Saur Energy that the company sees manufacturing and EPC as complementary capabilities. "Manufacturing is dedicated to creating volume production," Kabra said, but added that manufacturing "does not necessarily give them the knowledge about how these markets function and what their core needs are." “In the solar ecosystem, there are other components that add value, such as site assessment, structure, and design selection of the inverter among others. This is where EPC companies integrate the right technologies, design systems based on customer requirements and ensure seamless execution and long-term service,” Kabra added. GK's answer on financing is a blended model. The company plans to operate directly in selected markets while using partnerships and existing networks to expand its reach elsewhere. Kabra also sees service as an economic asset rather than simply a cost. "When the end-user has a great experience with the brand, it creates trust and loyalty," he said, arguing that sustainable margins come from efficient execution, service capabilities and reliable performance across the project's lifecycle. That is important because it complicates the supposed manufacturing-versus-service divide. The manufacturers entering rooftop are increasingly discovering that they cannot simply manufacture their way into the residential market. They need a service organisation too. Ever since, manufacturing companies that had been confined to one business alone are now diversifying. Take the case of the Indian solar glass manufacturer Borosil Renewables. The firm is now trying its hand at a pilot-based, low-risk model entry with co-branded execution before white-level investment. It has targeted the residential, Commercial & Industrial (C&I) and off-grid solar market in three states-Gujarat, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh. It has, as of now, adopted a dual-channel approach. One includes product distribution and the other is direct consumer engagement. However, it is a starting point now for the Mumbai-based firm. The top leadership of the firm said that it has planned to earn around Rs 36 crore in 2026-27 from the new vertical but admits that the margins will not be as high as what they get in solar glass manufacturing, but pointed out that the volumes can drive the growth. “We have started this new initiative to leverage the brand and to use the acceptability of product of the company and the group. And this is very early stage to see what would be the outcome finally. But our internal target is to generate revenue of about Rs 36 crores in this financial year. In the first quarter, the revenue was about INR1.3 crores. We have just started with small projects. And as we go along, the awareness will increase and our team has been already built up, so which will be obtaining more business, and we hope to do a good job here,” Ashok Jain , Whole Time Director of Borosil Renewables, said. Tata Power's hybrid model If there is one company that demonstrates how the two camps can begin to converge, it is Tata Power. The firm hopes to continue leading the market with 25% of India’s rooftop solar market by 2030. The company has built a large rooftop business without relying solely on a conventional employee-led EPC structure. Its channel-partner network, brand, technology, supply chain and after-sales systems have become important parts of its competitive proposition. And the financial performance shows why this strategy matters. In its Q1 FY27 investor call, Tata Power said rooftop revenue had grown nearly 100% year-on-year. Rooftop EBITDA had grown 68%, while profit had increased by more than 67%. The company also reported a four-year Q1 CAGR of 58% for revenue and 84% for PAT. Management expects rooftop growth of another 60%-70% this year. “Last year, we grew by 100%, and this year also, we have plans to grow by about 60% to 70%,” Praveer Sinha , Chairman and Managing Director (CMD) of Tata Power said in an investor call this month. He also added that with the firm adding battery storage to its menu, it expects that to power growth ahead as well. Being neither a pure service-first company nor simply a manufacturer selling equipment. Tata Power is building an ecosystem based on something rare in the solar chain: trust. The financing question This is why financing deserves to be treated as a separate axis of the rooftop battle. The traditional argument that solar is becoming cheaper misses the fact that the upfront ticket remains significant for an average household. Ecofy's experience shows how financing is evolving around that reality. Swapnil said customers increasingly want an "easy, paperless, digitized instant process". The NBFC can offer loan tenures from six to 60 months and products such as no-cost EMI. The customer mix also illustrates the importance of financing design. Around 30% of Ecofy's book is no-cost EMI, while the remaining 70% largely consists of customers who want longer tenures because they are effectively replacing their electricity bill with a solar EMI. Ajay Yadav, President of the Renewable Energy Association of Rajasthan (REAR), sees financing as one of the biggest operational bottlenecks in the PM Surya Ghar rollout. According to Yadav, around 80% of his clients take loans. Yet delays in bank processing can hold up projects after the customer has already decided to install solar. He described the banking process as cumbersome, with excessive compliance requirements and unnecessary visits, and said consumers and vendors increasingly prefer NBFCs because the process is faster and more convenient. This has an important implication for the business-model debate. The company that wins the rooftop customer may not necessarily be the one with the cheapest module. It may be the one that can say: this is the system, this is your EMI, this is when it will be installed, and this is who will service it. The channel is becoming the battleground This is where the growing manufacturer push into rooftop creates its most difficult challenge. Manufacturers need EPCs because they provide reach. EPCs need manufacturers because they provide equipment. But both increasingly want a relationship with the same customer. The emergence of manufacturer-led kits is one visible symptom of this larger tension, rather than the central story itself. Yadav said the increasing use of such bundled offerings is reducing the flexibility of some EPC companies, which traditionally select components according to the requirements of individual projects. He argued for an open-market system in which installers can choose components rather than being pushed towards a particular manufacturer's configuration. He also pointed to another problem: manufacturers advertising kit prices directly can create confusion for customers when those advertised prices are compared with an EPC's final quotation, which may include installation, structures and project-specific requirements. The tension is therefore not simply about procurement. It is about who gets to define the product. The manufacturer sees the product as a standardised system. The EPC sees it as an engineered solution for an individual roof. The customer wants a competitive price without having to understand the difference. That conflict is likely to become more important as manufacturers expand their retail ambitions. Where the two models converge Yet the market is already showing signs that neither extreme may win. Manufacturers are learning that customer acquisition and service cannot be ignored. Service-first companies are discovering that financing, technology and even private-label procurement can create stronger control over their economics. Some manufacturers are selling through independent installers rather than replacing them. Some installers are bundling storage and financing. And companies such as Tata Power are building hybrid ecosystems that combine manufacturing, brand, channel partners and after-sales capabilities. GK Energy's Kabra also expects consolidation as the sector matures, while arguing that engineering, execution and lifecycle support remain essential even when manufacturing is controlled by the same company. The question, then, is not whether manufacturing will replace service or whether service companies will defeat manufacturers. It is whether the two capabilities eventually become inseparable. The economics will decide The ultimate test will be margins. Residential rooftop EPC margins are already under pressure. Equipment prices are competitive, customer acquisition costs can be high and the cost of servicing thousands of geographically dispersed systems can accumulate over time. A manufacturer has an obvious advantage in controlling its BOM. But it also carries the capital intensity and operational complexity of manufacturing. A service-first company avoids that capital burden but remains exposed to equipment prices and supplier relationships. Its advantage is flexibility. The manufacturer can potentially capture margin at every layer. The service provider can potentially build a higher-value relationship with the customer. The financier cares about both. This is why Ecofy's preference for established installers and OEM-associated networks is significant. It suggests that service quality is beginning to influence not only customer choice but also the cost and availability of capital. As rooftop systems increasingly include batteries, the importance of installation quality and long-term service will only increase. The more complicated the system becomes, the less sustainable a purely transactional installation model is likely to be. Conclusion India's rooftop solar market faces two pathways. The first is that solar equipment will become increasingly commoditised and that the real competitive advantage will sit downstream — in financing, customer acquisition, installation quality, service and retention. The second is that control over manufacturing, supply chains and technology will provide enough economic and quality advantages to justify moving downstream into EPC and retail. Neither argument is obviously wrong. Tata Power's performance suggests what that convergence could look like: manufacturing and supply-chain control on one side; channel partners, digital systems, brand and after-sales on the other. Its management has argued that the company has built the supply chain, channel-partner network, after-sales service and digital infrastructure required to scale rooftop. GK Energy is pursuing a blended approach. Oswal Pumps and Shakti Pumps are moving deeper into manufacturing and EPC. Traditional installers continue to build their businesses around service and customer relationships. Most importantly, customers will increasingly start to value both visibility and longevity of the firm selling them the system, considering the promised life of the system itself at 25 years. That is the advantage Tata Power has milked for instance to charge a premium. Add to that, the lack of really strong benefits led to communication beyond price or savings, or matters like safety and service. As the market matures, more segments will seek those as well. India remains a far cry from the sophisticated communications we see in the developed markets, where solar is much more pricier, and with storage, could easily be 3-4x India’s typical comparable system costs. That leaves open the possibility of high quality advertising and communications allowing firms to charge a premium, as Solar Square does for instance. In every simulation, one thing is clear. The industry will not sustain the thousands of installers that populate the Pm Suryaghar dashboard and beyond for now. A few firms will grow much bigger, while we will see regional champions emerge as well, to leave the market with perhaps 150-300 at best, or even less than 100 firms eventually in a few years.

“We have started this new initiative to leverage the brand and to use the acceptability of product of the company and the group.
And this is very early stage to see what would be the outcome finally.
But our internal target is to generate revenue of about Rs 36 crores in this financial year.
In the first quarter, the revenue was about INR1.3 crores.
We have just started with small projects.

And as we go along, the awareness will increase and our team has been already built up, so which will be obtaining more business, and we hope to do a good job here,” Ashok Jain, Whole Time Director of Borosil Renewables, said.
Tata Power's hybrid model If there is one company that demonstrates how the two camps can begin to converge, it is Tata Power.
The firm hopes to continue leading the market with 25% of India’s rooftop solar market by 2030.
The company has built a large rooftop business without relying solely on a conventional employee-led EPC structure.
Its channel-partner network, brand, technology, supply chain and after-sales systems have become important parts of its competitive proposition.
And the financial performance shows why this strategy matters.
In its Q1 FY27 investor call, Tata Power said rooftop revenue had grown nearly 100% year-on-year.
The company also reported a four-year Q1 CAGR of 58% for revenue and 84% for PAT.
Management expects rooftop growth of another 60%-70% this year.
He also added that with the firm adding battery storage to its menu, it expects that to power growth ahead as well.
Being neither a pure service-first company nor simply a manufacturer selling equipment.
Tata Power is building an ecosystem based on something rare in the solar chain: trust.
The financing question This is why financing deserves to be treated as a separate axis of the rooftop battle.
The traditional argument that solar is becoming cheaper misses the fact that the upfront ticket remains significant for an average household.
Ecofy's experience shows how financing is evolving around that reality.
Swapnil said customers increasingly want an "easy, paperless, digitized instant process".
The NBFC can offer loan tenures from six to 60 months and products such as no-cost EMI.
The customer mix also illustrates the importance of financing design.

Around 30% of Ecofy's book is no-cost EMI, while the remaining 70% largely consists of customers who want longer tenures because they are effectively replacing their electricity bill with a solar EMI.
Ajay Yadav, President of the Renewable Energy Association of Rajasthan (REAR), sees financing as one of the biggest operational bottlenecks in the PM Surya Ghar rollout.
According to Yadav, around 80% of his clients take loans.
Yet delays in bank processing can hold up projects after the customer has already decided to install solar.

He described the banking process as cumbersome, with excessive compliance requirements and unnecessary visits, and said consumers and vendors increasingly prefer NBFCs because the process is faster and more convenient.
This has an important implication for the business-model debate.
The company that wins the rooftop customer may not necessarily be the one with the cheapest module.
It may be the one that can say: this is the system, this is your EMI, this is when it will be installed, and this is who will service it.
The channel is becoming the battleground This is where the growing manufacturer push into rooftop creates its most difficult challenge.
Manufacturers need EPCs because they provide reach.
EPCs need manufacturers because they provide equipment.
But both increasingly want a relationship with the same customer.
The emergence of manufacturer-led kits is one visible symptom of this larger tension, rather than the central story itself.
Yadav said the increasing use of such bundled offerings is reducing the flexibility of some EPC companies, which traditionally select components according to the requirements of individual projects.
He argued for an open-market system in which installers can choose components rather than being pushed towards a particular manufacturer's configuration.

He also pointed to another problem: manufacturers advertising kit prices directly can create confusion for customers when those advertised prices are compared with an EPC's final quotation, which may include installation, structures and project-specific requirements.
The tension is therefore not simply about procurement.
It is about who gets to define the product.
The manufacturer sees the product as a standardised system.
The EPC sees it as an engineered solution for an individual roof.
The customer wants a competitive price without having to understand the difference.
That conflict is likely to become more important as manufacturers expand their retail ambitions.
Where the two models converge Yet the market is already showing signs that neither extreme may win.
Manufacturers are learning that customer acquisition and service cannot be ignored.
Service-first companies are discovering that financing, technology and even private-label procurement can create stronger control over their economics.
Some manufacturers are selling through independent installers rather than replacing them.
Some installers are bundling storage and financing.
And companies such as Tata Power are building hybrid ecosystems that combine manufacturing, brand, channel partners and after-sales capabilities.

GK Energy's Kabra also expects consolidation as the sector matures, while arguing that engineering, execution and lifecycle support remain essential even when manufacturing is controlled by the same company.
The question, then, is not whether manufacturing will replace service or whether service companies will defeat manufacturers.
It is whether the two capabilities eventually become inseparable.
The economics will decide The ultimate test will be margins.
Residential rooftop EPC margins are already under pressure.
Equipment prices are competitive, customer acquisition costs can be high and the cost of servicing thousands of geographically dispersed systems can accumulate over time.
A manufacturer has an obvious advantage in controlling its BOM.
But it also carries the capital intensity and operational complexity of manufacturing.
A service-first company avoids that capital burden but remains exposed to equipment prices and supplier relationships.
Its advantage is flexibility.
The manufacturer can potentially capture margin at every layer.
The service provider can potentially build a higher-value relationship with the customer.
The financier cares about both.
This is why Ecofy's preference for established installers and OEM-associated networks is significant.
It suggests that service quality is beginning to influence not only customer choice but also the cost and availability of capital.
As rooftop systems increasingly include batteries, the importance of installation quality and long-term service will only increase.
The more complicated the system becomes, the less sustainable a purely transactional installation model is likely to be.
Conclusion India's rooftop solar market faces two pathways.

The first is that solar equipment will become increasingly commoditised and that the real competitive advantage will sit downstream — in financing, customer acquisition, installation quality, service and retention.
The second is that control over manufacturing, supply chains and technology will provide enough economic and quality advantages to justify moving downstream into EPC and retail.
Neither argument is obviously wrong.
Tata Power's performance suggests what that convergence could look like: manufacturing and supply-chain control on one side; channel partners, digital systems, brand and after-sales on the other.
Its management has argued that the company has built the supply chain, channel-partner network, after-sales service and digital infrastructure required to scale rooftop.
GK Energy is pursuing a blended approach.
Oswal Pumps and Shakti Pumps are moving deeper into manufacturing and EPC.
Traditional installers continue to build their businesses around service and customer relationships.
Most importantly, customers will increasingly start to value both visibility and longevity of the firm selling them the system, considering the promised life of the system itself at 25 years.
That is the advantage Tata Power has milked for instance to charge a premium.
Add to that, the lack of really strong benefits led to communication beyond price or savings, or matters like safety and service.
As the market matures, more segments will seek those as well.

India remains a far cry from the sophisticated communications we see in the developed markets, where solar is much more pricier, and with storage, could easily be 3-4x India’s typical comparable system costs.
That leaves open the possibility of high quality advertising and communications allowing firms to charge a premium, as Solar Square does for instance.
In every simulation, one thing is clear.
The industry will not sustain the thousands of installers that populate the Pm Suryaghar dashboard and beyond for now.
A few firms will grow much bigger, while we will see regional champions emerge as well, to leave the market with perhaps 150-300 at best, or even less than 100 firms eventually in a few years.

stories.headline: Repeated closures undermine Mughal Road’s promise as Kashmir’s alternate highway
stories.title: Repeated closures undermine Mughal Road’s promise as Kashmir’s alternate highway
stories.summary: Shopian, Aug 26: The Mughal Road, touted as an alternative link between Kashmir and the Jammu region, has faced repeated disruptions this summer due to cloudbursts and landslides, raising questions over its reliability as an all-weather route. On August 5, Chief Minister Omar Abdullah travelled to Rajouri and Poonch through the historic road and later described its condition as worse than the Jammu-Srinagar National Highway, which had itself been battered by torrential rain and landslides. The Mughal Road connects south Kashmir’s Shopian district with Poonch in the Jammu region, cutting across the Pir Panjal range. The road was thrown open to vehicular traffic in 2009 and was projected as an alternative link to the Jammu-Srinagar National Highway. However, repeated weather-related disruptions have limited its potential as a dependable alternative route. Since June, the road has witnessed several cloudbursts and landslides. Official records show that a cloudburst occurred at Zaznar Point on June 29, while another hit the Sukh Sarai area on June 14. A landslide was subsequently reported in the Lal Ghulam area on July 14, followed by another in the Sukh Sarai area on August 3, disrupting traffic along the route. Despite the repeated incidents, authorities have been working to restore connectivity at the earliest. An official from the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) said the 52 RCC under Project Beacon has been clearing the road immediately after blockages. “Our teams respond immediately whenever the road is blocked. The priority is to clear debris and restore traffic at the earliest,” the official said. The road’s vulnerability, however, is not limited to the summer months. Mughal Road remains closed for more than four months during winter because of heavy snowfall around Peer Ki Gali, located at an elevation of around 11,500 feet. The seasonal closure limits its usefulness as a reliable alternative to the national highway, particularly during periods when the main Jammu-Srinagar route is disrupted. For residents and traders in Shopian, Rajouri and Poonch, the road is an important connectivity link, providing a shorter route between the two regions. “The road is important for people on both sides of the Pir Panjal, but frequent closures make it difficult to depend on it for regular travel and transportation,” said Mohammad Ashraf, a local resident. The route also has economic significance for south Kashmir’s horticulture sector, as it provides access to markets in the Jammu region. The repeated disruptions have assumed greater significance as the Jammu-Srinagar National Highway itself remains vulnerable to landslides, shooting stones and extreme weather. Mughal Road could provide an important alternative during such disruptions, particularly for traffic between south Kashmir and the Pir Panjal districts. But its own exposure to cloudbursts, landslides and heavy snowfall limits the extent to which it can perform that role. However, officials said that a proposed 9-km tunnel between Chatta Pani in Poonch and Zaznar in Shopian could eventually address the Mughal Road’s biggest weakness of its prolonged winter closures and vulnerability to extreme weather. The Centre approved the Pir Ki Gali tunnel project in June 2025 at an estimated cost of around Rs 3830 crore, with the tunnel envisaged as an all-weather link between the Kashmir Valley and the Pir Panjal region. “Once completed, it would bypass the high-altitude Pir Ki Gali stretch, where heavy snowfall regularly disrupts traffic for several months,” said the officials.

Mughal Road remains closed for more than four months during winter because of heavy snowfall around Peer Ki Gali, located at an elevation of around 11,500 feet.

But its own exposure to cloudbursts, landslides and heavy snowfall limits the extent to which it can perform that role.

The Centre approved the Pir Ki Gali tunnel project in June 2025 at an estimated cost of around Rs 3830 crore, with the tunnel envisaged as an all-weather link between the Kashmir Valley and the Pir Panjal region.
“Once completed, it would bypass the high-altitude Pir Ki Gali stretch, where heavy snowfall regularly disrupts traffic for several months,” said the officials.
